content: Cefuroxime axetil is an oral antibiotic classified as a second-generation cephalosporin. It is FDA-approved for treating various bacterial infections, including pharyngitis/tonsillitis, acute bacterial otitis media, acute bacterial maxillary sinusitis, acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, secondary bacterial infections of acute bronchitis, uncomplicated skin and skin-structure infections, uncomplicated urinary tract infections, uncomplicated gonorrhea, early Lyme disease (erythema migrans), and impetigo. Adult Indications and Dosage Cefuroxime axetil should only be used to treat or prevent infections caused by bacteria proven or strongly suspected to be susceptible to the drug. When available, culture and susceptibility data should guide therapy selection. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may inform empiric therapy. Cefuroxime Axetil Tablets Cefuroxime axetil tablets are indicated for treating mild to moderate infections caused by susceptible strains of designated microorganisms in specific conditions: Pharyngitis/Tonsillitis: Caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. Note that penicillin is the preferred drug for treating and preventing streptococcal infections, including rheumatic fever prophylaxis. Cefuroxime axetil is effective in eradicating streptococci from the nasopharynx, but its efficacy in preventing rheumatic fever is not established. Acute Bacterial Maxillary Sinusitis: Caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae (non-beta-lactamase-producing strains only). The effectiveness of cefuroxime axetil for sinus infections caused by beta-lactamase-producing strains of H. influenzae or Moraxella catarrhalis could not be adequately evaluated due to insufficient clinical trial data. Acute Bacterial Otitis Media: Caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (including beta-lactamase-producing strains), Moraxella catarrhalis (including beta-lactamase-producing strains), or Streptococcus pyogenes. Uncomplicated Skin and Skin-Structure Infections: Caused by Staphylococcus aureus (including beta-lactamase-producing strains) or Streptococcus pyogenes. Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections: Caused by Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae. Uncomplicated Gonorrhea: Caused by penicillinase-producing and non-penicillinase-producing strains of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Early Lyme Disease (Erythema Migrans): Caused by Borrelia burgdorferi. Dosage Adjustments Cefuroxime is primarily eliminated by the kidneys. Dosage adjustments are required for patients with a creatinine clearance of less than 30 mL/min. Pediatric Indications and Dosage Cefuroxime axetil oral suspension is indicated for pediatric patients aged 3 months to 12 years with mild to moderate infections caused by susceptible strains of designated microorganisms. The safety and effectiveness of cefuroxime axetil for infections other than those listed have not been established. Preparation of Oral Suspension Shake the bottle to loosen the powder. Add the specified amount of water for reconstitution, replace the cap, and shake vigorously. Store the reconstituted suspension in a refrigerator (2°C to 8°C) and discard after 10 days. Contraindications Cefuroxime axetil is contraindicated in patients with known allergies to cephalosporins. Warnings and Precautions Hypersensitivity Reactions: Cross-reactivity with penicillins may occur in up to 10% of penicillin-allergic patients. If an allergic reaction occurs, discontinue the drug and initiate appropriate therapy. Clostridium difficile-Associated Diarrhea (CDAD): CDAD has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefuroxime axetil. If CDAD is suspected, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Superinfection: Prolonged use may result in overgrowth of nonsusceptible microorganisms. If superinfection occurs, appropriate measures should be taken. Renal Function: Use with caution in patients receiving potent diuretics, as these may adversely affect renal function. Prothrombin Time Monitoring: Cephalosporins may be associated with a fall in prothrombin activity. Monitor prothrombin time in at-risk patients and administer vitamin K as indicated. Adverse Reactions Clinical Trials: Common adverse reactions include gastrointestinal disturbances such as diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. The incidence of gastrointestinal events increases with higher doses. Postmarketing Experience: Reported events include hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis, angioedema, rash), pseudomembranous colitis, hemolytic anemia, hepatic impairment, seizures, and severe skin reactions (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis). Drug Interactions Concomitant administration of probenecid increases serum concentrations of cefuroxime. Drugs that reduce gastric acidity may lower the bioavailability of cefuroxime axetil. Cefuroxime axetil may affect gut flora, potentially reducing the efficacy of oral contraceptives. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Classified as Category B by the FDA. Animal studies have not shown evidence of harm to the fetus, but adequate studies in pregnant women are lacking. Nursing Mothers: Cefuroxime is excreted in human milk. Consider discontinuing nursing temporarily during treatment. Pediatric Use: Safety and effectiveness have been established for children aged 3 months to 12 years. Geriatric Use: No significant differences in safety or effectiveness were observed between elderly and younger adult patients. Overdosage Overdosage of cephalosporins can cause cerebral irritation leading to seizures or encephalopathy. Hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis can reduce serum levels of cefuroxime. Mechanism of Action Cefuroxime axetil is a bactericidal agent that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis. It remains active in the presence of some beta-lactamases produced by Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Microbiology Cefuroxime axetil is effective against a range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible isolates), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, and Haemophilus influenzae. Resistance mechanisms include beta-lactamase hydrolysis, altered penicillin-binding proteins, and decreased permeability. Administration and Monitoring Cefuroxime axetil is administered orally as tablets or oral suspension. Prothrombin time should be monitored in at-risk patients, and vitamin K administered as needed.
